text:
The Long Way Home: Apollo 13

On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted from Florida carrying three men toward the Moon. Jim Lovell, the commander, was making his fourth spaceflight and his second trip around the Moon. Fred Haise was a rookie, assigned to pilot the lunar module. The third seat belonged to Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days earlier. The original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles and grounded by flight surgeons. Swigert trained hard and learned the job in a hurry. Nobody yet knew how much that last-minute swap would matter.

Public interest in Apollo had already faded. Apollo 11 had made the landing feel routine, and the networks did not carry the crew's television broadcast on the night of April 13. Almost no one was watching when the trouble began.

The seeds had been planted long before launch. The spacecraft carried its oxygen and hydrogen in insulated tanks, and these fed the fuel cells that made the ship's electricity and drinking water. One oxygen tank had been dropped slightly during handling at the factory. Later, during a ground test, technicians had trouble emptying it, so they ran heaters inside the tank for hours, using a power supply stronger than the tank's wiring was built for. The heat fused the protective switches shut and baked the Teflon insulation on the internal wires. Nobody noticed. The tank passed inspection and flew.

Fifty-five hours into the mission, the crew was about 200,000 miles from Earth. Mission Control asked them to stir the tanks, a routine step that keeps the supercold contents from settling. Swigert flipped the switch. A spark jumped across the damaged wires, the Teflon caught fire in the pure oxygen, and pressure inside the tank surged. A moment later the tank burst.

The crew felt a bang and a shudder. Swigert reported first, saying that they had a problem. Lovell repeated it for the people on the ground. Warning lights flickered across the panel and the voltage dropped. Then Lovell looked out the window and saw a stream of gas pouring into space. The second oxygen tank was emptying too. The explosion had also blown a panel off the side of the service module, though the crew would not see that damage for days.

In Houston, flight controllers watched their screens fall apart. At first they suspected bad instruments, because it seemed impossible that so many systems could fail at once. Within minutes the truth was plain. The fuel cells were dying, the oxygen was almost gone, and the command module, named Odyssey, would soon have no power at all. Without it, the crew could not survive reentry. Gene Kranz, the flight director, gathered his teams and told them to work the problem calmly and keep the crew alive.

The answer lay in the lunar module, named Aquarius, still docked to the front of the command module. It had its own oxygen, water, batteries and engine, all designed to support two men for two days on the Moon. Now it would have to sustain three men for four days, serving as a lifeboat. Lovell and Haise powered it up while Swigert shut down Odyssey, preserving what little battery charge it had for the final minutes before landing. The landing on the Moon was abandoned. The goal now was simply to get home.

That was harder than it sounds. The spacecraft was on a path that would loop it around the Moon and, if nothing else were done, carry it back toward Earth. But the path would miss the planet by a wide margin, and the service module engine could not be trusted after the blast. Controllers decided to use the lunar module's descent engine, a machine built for landing, to reshape the trajectory. A first burn put the ship on course to return. After swinging around the far side of the Moon, where the crew were farther from home than any humans had ever been, a second burn shortened the trip by about ten hours. Fuel mattered, but so did the clock, because the lunar module's supplies would not last.

Trouble followed trouble. The lunar module's air was cleaned by canisters of lithium hydroxide, which absorb the carbon dioxide the crew exhaled. Aquarius had enough canisters for two men for two days, and those were filling up. Spare canisters existed in Odyssey, but they were square and the lunar module's sockets were round. On the ground, engineers dumped onto a table the same odds and ends the astronauts had aboard, including plastic bags, cardboard, hoses and duct tape. They built an adapter and read the instructions to the crew over the radio. The astronauts copied it, and the carbon dioxide level began to fall.

Cold set in as well. To save power, the crew switched off almost everything, including the heaters. The cabin dropped to a little above freezing, water condensed on the walls, and the men slept little in their thin flight suits. Water was rationed to a few ounces a day, and Haise developed a fever from an infection. They were tired, thirsty and chilled, and the Earth ahead of them looked small.

Meanwhile, Mattingly and a team of engineers worked in simulators in Houston to write a new procedure for restarting Odyssey. It had to be done with the tiny electrical budget that remained, in an order never planned or tested, and it had to work the first time. They finished it and read it up to the crew.

On the last day, one more correction was needed. The ship had drifted slightly off its path, and a reentry angle that was too shallow would skip it off the atmosphere into space, while one too steep would burn it up. With the guidance computer unavailable, Lovell steered by hand. He lined up the spacecraft by watching the edge of daylight on the Earth and fired the engine for a few seconds, exactly as rehearsed on the ground.

About four hours before reentry, the crew released the service module. For the first time they could see what the explosion had done. One entire side panel was gone, and wiring and equipment hung exposed. Lovell described it to the ground, and engineers finally understood how violent the accident had been. Then, with Odyssey's batteries warmed and brought back to life by the new procedure, the crew left Aquarius and let it go. The lunar module, which had saved them, burned up in the atmosphere over the Pacific.

Reentry brought the last silence. Every returning spacecraft passes through a few minutes of radio blackout as superheated air wraps the capsule. The expected blackout came and went. The time ran longer. In Mission Control, no one spoke. Then, a minute later than predicted, Swigert's voice crackled through the static. Three parachutes appeared, bright against the sky.

Odyssey splashed down in the South Pacific on April 17, 1970, near the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima. The mission had lasted almost six days. The crew were thin, dehydrated and exhausted, but alive. The ground teams in Houston, who had hardly slept, burst into cheers and tears.

Apollo 13 never reached the Moon, and in the sense that counted, it was still a success. A review board traced the failure to the damaged tank and its wiring, and the design was changed for later flights. The episode showed how much could be done by people who refused to quit and who thought clearly under pressure. NASA later called the mission a successful failure, and the name stuck because it was exactly right.
